opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That project was really my first taste of what machine learning could do for science, and it ended up shaping a lot of how I think about AI even today.

At the time I was an undergraduate studying physics, and in high-energy physics one of the big bottlenecks is simulation. When you want to understand what happens in a particle collision, you need to simulate how particles shower through the detector, and doing that with traditional Monte Carlo methods is extremely expensive computationally. So the idea was: can we use a generative model, a GAN, to learn the distribution of these detector responses and then generate samples much faster?

What struck me was two things. First, it actually kind of worked. A neural network that knew nothing about physics could produce outputs that looked surprisingly similar to the real simulations. That was exciting and a little bit shocking to me as a physics student, because I had been trained to believe you understand the world by writing down equations from first principles.

But the second thing was a sense of discomfort. When the GAN produced something, I didn't really know why. It was a black box. As a physicist, you're not satisfied just matching a distribution; you want to know what the model has learned, whether it respects conservation laws and symmetries, and whether you can trust it outside the regime you trained it on. GANs were also notoriously unstable to train, so a lot of the work felt more like alchemy than science.

That tension really stuck with me. On one hand, AI is clearly a powerful tool for science. On the other hand, if we want to use it for science, we need it to be interpretable, and ideally we want to understand AI itself in a scientific way, the way a physicist understands a physical system. I think that's the seed of a lot of what I've worked on since: bringing physics intuition into AI, building models that are more interpretable, and trying to treat neural networks as objects we can study and understand rather than just use.

So in a sense that first project gave me both the excitement and the question. The excitement was "this is powerful," and the question was "but what is it actually doing?" I've been chasing that question ever since.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the project sparked interest in AI and shaped later work, but does not attribute a shift toward AI to finding it more personally rewarding than studying physics.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That project was actually my first real brush with AI, and it came from a pretty practical place. I was an undergraduate at Peking University doing physics, and the group I was in cared about simulating detector data for high-energy physics experiments. The standard simulations were extremely expensive computationally, and the idea at the time was: could a generative model, a GAN, learn the distribution of those events and produce them much faster?

What hooked me wasn't really the physics result. It was watching the model learn. You'd train it, and at first it produced garbage, and then slowly the distributions started to look like the real detector output. For someone trained in physics, where you usually write down the equations first and then compute, this was backwards. The machine was finding structure without being told what the structure was. That felt almost magical, and also a little unsettling.

The second thing it taught me was how fragile these models can be. GANs are notoriously hard to train. Mode collapse, instability, all of that. As a physicist I wanted to understand why. Why does this loss landscape behave this way? Is there a principle underneath it? I couldn't get satisfying answers, and that gap stuck with me. I think it's why I eventually gravitated toward interpretability and toward thinking about neural networks the way a physicist thinks about a physical system, something to be understood with laws and mechanisms, not just used.

So in a sense that undergraduate project set up the two questions I'm still working on: can AI help us do science, and can we do science on AI itself.

r001.rationale: The response says watching the GAN learn hooked him and later drew him toward interpretability, but it does not attribute his shift toward AI to finding learning AI more personally rewarding than studying physics.

That tension drew me toward AI itself—not just using it as a tool, but trying to understand it scientifically.

sol-6.1.text: That project was really my entry point into AI. I was interested in physics, and GANs gave me a way to explore how a model could learn from data and generate something new. What fascinated me was the connection between a relatively simple objective and the complex behavior that could emerge from training. It shifted my curiosity from just using the model for a physics problem to asking how the model itself worked—what it was learning, why it worked, and where it failed. That became a motivation to explore AI more deeply.
